strengths: Holistic approach to cross-modal integration: Rather than relying on simple late-stage LLM concatenation, the paper proposes a coordinated framework spanning early text-guided vision encoding, recursive context-aware decoding layers, bidirectional semantic mapping loss, and synthetic data generation.

Strong empirical performance: Across a comprehensive suite of 22 multimodal benchmarks, FUSION models (at 3B and 8B scales) achieve competitive or superior performance compared to strong baselines (e.g., Cambrian-1, Florence-VL, LLaVA-OneVision) while utilizing significantly fewer visual tokens (620 and 300 tokens).

Thorough ablation studies: The authors provide detailed ablation experiments validating the individual contributions of each architectural module (Table 2 and Table 4), the effect of synthetic data across stages (Table 3), latent token counts and window sizes (Tables 5-7, 10), and parameter freezing strategies (Table 8).

Detailed appendix and data generation pipeline: The methodology behind prompt design, multi-stage filtering (rule-based, LLM scoring, SSIM, ClipScore), and dataset distribution is thoroughly documented.
weaknesses: Inference latency and computational overhead of query-dependent encoding: Because the vision encoder is conditioned on the input question text (Text-Guided Unified Vision Encoding), the image cannot be pre-encoded once and cached across multiple questions or multi-turn dialogues. In scenarios where multiple questions are asked about the same image, this requires repeated forward passes through the visual backbone ($O(Q)$ vs. $O(1)$ image encodings), which significantly impacts serving throughput.

Architectural complexity: The pipeline introduces numerous interlocking modules and hyperparameters—such as text-to-vision projections, auxiliary partitioned image features ($I_A$), windowed attention, latent tokens $I_C$ with dynamic sampling, and dual mapping MLPs. The necessity of some intricate designs (e.g., partitioning into 4 sub-images for $I_A$) feels somewhat ad-hoc.

Cycle-consistency framing: The Dual-Supervised Semantic Mapping Loss essentially acts as an embedding cycle-consistency reconstruction objective, but it lacks deeper theoretical analysis or comparison against standard contrastive/projection alignment objectives used in prior literature.

Minor presentation and grammatical flaws: Several grammatical errors appear throughout the manuscript, including the title ('Fully Integration of...' instead of 'Full Integration of...') and section introductions ('we introduces', 'we proposes', 'we defines' in Section 3).

strengths: Comprehensive full-pipeline vision-language integration: The paper introduces multimodal interaction at multiple stages—early text-guided vision encoding, a bidirectional semantic mapping loss, and context-aware recursive decoding via latent tokens.

Strong empirical results with fewer visual tokens: Across 20+ multimodal benchmarks, the models achieve competitive or superior performance to existing methods (e.g., Florence-VL, Cambrian-1) while requiring significantly fewer visual tokens (620 or 300 tokens).

Thorough ablation studies: The authors provide detailed ablations examining individual architectural modules, latent token scaling, attention window sizes, synthetic data mixtures, and parameter-freezing strategies.

Effective data curation pipeline: The manuscript introduces a systematic language-first data generation and filtering framework leveraging generative models (FLUX, LLaMA-3.1-70B) with multi-stage verification.
weaknesses: Inference latency and caching limitations: Because the vision encoder is conditioned directly on the textual question via cross-attention, image representations cannot be pre-computed and cached independently of user prompts. This incurs significant computational overhead and latency in multi-turn dialogues or multi-query setups, which is acknowledged in the appendix but not quantitatively benchmarked.

Modest architectural gains under controlled settings: In the controlled ablation study on identical data and backbones (Table 2), the full model improves over the baseline Open LLaVA-NeXT by modest margins (e.g., from 74.4 to 74.9 on MMBench-EN, and 69.8 to 63.6 on TextVQA, which actually drops). This suggests that much of the large gains in Table 1 stem from the stronger vision backbone (SigLIP2-Giant) and extensive pretraining/tuning data rather than the architectural modifications alone.

Unclear computational and training cost details: The framework unfreezes all parameters (LLM and vision encoder) across all three training stages over 21M total training samples. Details regarding total GPU hours, FLOPs, and relative computational cost compared to frozen-encoder baselines are lacking.

Presentation and writing polish: The paper contains several grammatical errors and typos (e.g., 'Fully Integration' in the title should be 'Full Integration'; 'maximun value' on page 7; subject-verb agreement errors like 'we introduces', 'we proposes', 'we defines' on page 4; 'experimentss' on page 17).

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering 22 diverse multimodal benchmarks across general understanding, OCR/chart reasoning, knowledge-based reasoning, and vision-centric tasks.

Extensive ablation studies across components (TUNE, CARD, DSM), latent token counts, window sizes, and training stage freezing strategies, providing clear insights into how each part impacts performance.
Competitive performance achieved with a relatively compact visual token budget (620 and 300 tokens) compared to earlier models of comparable parameter scale.
Detailed appendix documenting the synthetic dataset creation pipeline, prompts, and multi-stage filtering heuristics.
weaknesses: Fundamental practical and architectural drawback: Injecting text into the vision encoder (Text-Guided Unified Vision Encoding) ties visual feature extraction directly to the question prompt. This completely invalidates image feature caching across multi-turn dialogues or multiple queries on the same image, requiring costly full re-runs of the vision backbone for every single question. The paper fails to discuss or benchmark this computational and latency overhead.

Lack of inference latency, throughput, and computational cost profiling: Despite claiming high efficiency with fewer vision tokens, the architecture introduces text-guided vision encoding, auxiliary non-conditioned visual encoding (IA), and repeated cross-attention interaction layers throughout LLM decoding. The paper provides no empirical measurements of runtime FLOPs, memory footprint, or tokens-per-second generation speeds compared to standard projector-based MLLMs.

Mathematical imprecision and ambiguous formulation: In Equations (12) and (13), the loss terms compute cosine similarities between sequences/matrices ($E_{txt}$, $V^f_{txt}$, $E_{img}$, $V_{img}$), but the notation treats them as single vectors without defining how aggregation, sequence-length matching, or spatial pooling is conducted across token dimensions.

Limited conceptual novelty: The core elements largely assemble known techniques—early vision-text interaction (analogous to Q-Former/Q-ViT), interleaved cross-attention decoding layers (similar to Flamingo/IDEFICS), bidirectional projection cycle consistency (SEA), and diffusion-based synthetic data generation (SynthVLM)—without offering fundamentally novel architectural insights.

Unfair baseline comparisons: The strongest results (FUSION-X) rely on the newly released SigLIP2-Giant backbone, whereas direct baselines like Cambrian-1 and Florence-VL are evaluated with older, less capable encoders. Additionally, all model parameters (LLM and vision encoder) are fully fine-tuned across three stages with over 21M samples, confounding whether gains arise from the proposed architecture or from the aggressive full-parameter fine-tuning and updated vision encoder.

Clarity and presentation issues: The paper exhibits noticeable grammatical and editorial oversights, starting from the paper title ('Fully Integration...' instead of 'Full Integration'), down to several typos and grammatical errors in the text (e.g., 'In 3.1, we introduces...', 'In 3.2, we proposes...', 'inconsisten cies', 'maximun').

strengths: Holistic multimodal integration framework: The paper systematically tackles the problem of modality isolation across three levels—early vision encoding (Text-Guided Vision Encoding), projection (Dual-Semantic Mapping Loss), and decoding (Context-Aware Alignment Decoding with semantic exchange layers).

Extensive empirical evaluation: The proposed FLARE models (at 3B and 8B scales, in fixed-token and dynamic-token configurations) are evaluated across 16 standard multimodal benchmarks spanning general perception, OCR/chart reasoning, domain knowledge, and vision-centric tasks.

Well-structured ablation studies and controlled experiments: The paper includes component-wise ablations (Table 3), controlled evaluations isolating architecture differences on fixed datasets such as Open-LLaVA-NeXT-1M and Cambrian-1 7M (Table 4), and detailed cost/FLOPs analyses (Tables 5 and 6).

Data synthesis and filtering pipeline: The appendix provides extensive details on the text-driven synthetic data generation framework, prompt designs across multiple QA formats, and quantitative filtering metrics (CLIPScore, SSIM, human and automated evaluations).
weaknesses: Query-dependent vision encoding hinders feature caching: In standard VLM serving and multi-turn conversations, computing vision representations once per image and caching them is vital for throughput. Conditioning the vision encoder directly on textual query embeddings ($T_q$) requires re-encoding the image for each new or revised query, increasing practical serving latency. The manuscript lacks discussion and empirical profiling of this limitation in multi-turn scenarios.

Unclear inference details for dynamic latent tokens: During training, latent tokens are dynamically sampled from {4, 16, 36, 64, 144}. However, the paper does not clearly specify what fixed or adaptive configuration is used during evaluation across the 16 benchmarks in Tables 1, 2, and 4, which affects reproducibility and latency understanding.

Confounding contributions between architecture and synthetic data: While Table 7 isolates the synthetic data on FLARE, it is unclear how much existing baselines (e.g., LLaVA-NeXT) would gain if trained on the same synthesized data mix, making it difficult to fully disentangle the architectural gains from data-driven gains in the main benchmark comparisons.

Presentation and citation anomalies: The title contains a grammatical mistake ('Fully Integration' instead of 'Full Integration'), and several bibliographic entries list future publication years (e.g., '2026', '2026a', '2026b' in references for Lin et al. and Liu et al.).

strengths: Comprehensive and holistic integration framework: Rather than relying solely on a projection layer or late-stage LLM attention, the paper addresses cross-modal fusion across multiple stages—early text-guided vision encoding, a bidirectional dual-semantic mapping loss, and context-aware decoding via semantic exchange layers.

Rigorous and fair experimental setup: In addition to standard benchmark comparisons across 16 benchmarks, the authors conduct controlled evaluations holding the backbones and training datasets fixed (e.g., Qwen2.5VL backbone comparison in Table 2 and controlled datasets in Table 4), cleanly isolating architectural improvements.

Thorough ablation and computational efficiency analysis: The manuscript reports parameter ablations, FLOPs, wall-clock training time, and inference latency (Tables 5 and 6), demonstrating that FLARE-L achieves strong performance while using significantly fewer visual tokens and lower overall computational overhead than multi-encoder or dynamic-resolution baselines.

Well-documented data generation pipeline: The text-driven VQA synthesis approach and multi-stage filtering protocol are explained thoroughly with prompts, statistical distributions, and qualitative samples in the appendix.
weaknesses: Incompatibility with visual token caching in multi-turn conversations: Because textual query tokens are injected directly into the vision encoder at the initial encoding stage, image representations become query-dependent. Consequently, the vision encoder must be re-run for every turn or question about the same image, preventing standard image embedding reuse/caching and potentially increasing inference latency in interactive multi-turn dialogue scenarios.

Imprecise mathematical formalization in modality mapping: In Equation 4 and 5, visual features $V^e_i$ are formed by channel concatenation of shallow and deep features, thereby doubling the channel dimension. In Equation 9, $V^r_i = \text{MLP}_{t2v}(T_i)$ is compared against $V_i$ via cosine similarity. It is unclear whether $V_i$ refers to raw patch embeddings $V_i^0$ or encoded features $V_i^e$, and how dimension matching between the projected space and the target space is handled.

Handling of 2D spatial position embeddings in early ViT fusion: The paper concatenates Text2Vision embeddings $V_q$ with visual tokens $V_i$ before running the vision encoder layers. The paper does not clarify how 2D positional embeddings of standard ViT architectures (e.g., SigLIP2) are preserved or adapted when variable-length query tokens are appended.

Writing and grammatical slips: There is an evident grammatical error in the title ('FULLY INTEGRATION' instead of 'FULL INTEGRATION'), along with a few minor typos throughout the manuscript (e.g., 'synthesize corresponding images' vs 'synthesizing', inconsistent capitalization, and notation references).

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across a wide range of standard multimodal benchmarks (16 distinct benchmarks spanning general VLM capabilities, OCR/chart understanding, knowledge-intensive tasks, and vision-centric evaluation).
Detailed appendix documenting data generation prompts, filtering thresholds, and implementation details for the synthetic data generation pipeline.
Ablation studies examining various architectural hyperparameters, including layer placement intervals, latent token sample sizes, and the loss weighting coefficient lambda.
weaknesses: Severe practical limitation in deployment and multi-turn efficiency: Text-Guided Vision Encoding injects query embeddings directly into the vision encoder (Equations 1–4). In practical VLM deployments, image embeddings and KV caches are computed once and reused across multiple conversation turns and queries. By conditioning the vision encoder on the textual query, the model must re-encode high-resolution visual inputs for every new question or turn, dramatically inflating computational cost in interactive scenarios.

Methodological confounding and questionable comparisons: The paper bundles four distinct components (text-guided encoding, context-aware decoding, dual-semantic mapping loss, and large-scale synthetic data generation). In main benchmark comparisons (Table 1), it is impossible to disentangle how much of the performance gain stems from architecture versus the synthesized dataset. Furthermore, Table 2 claims an 'Architectural Comparison with Qwen2.5VL using identical backbones', but Qwen2.5VL was trained on trillions of tokens with proprietary recipes; it is unclear whether the authors re-trained Qwen2.5VL from scratch under identical training budgets or simply evaluated pre-trained weights against their own differently trained model.

Limited technical novelty: Each core component represents an incremental modification of existing paradigms. Early text-vision concatenation resembles classic early-fusion models (e.g., VL-BERT, UNITER); the semantic exchange layer between LLM decoding blocks is fundamentally similar to Flamingo's interleaved gated cross-attention; the dual-semantic mapping loss is a standard cycle-consistency cosine objective; and diffusion-based image-QA synthesis follows existing recipes like SynthVLM and ALLaVA.

Incomplete component ablations: In Table 3, the ablation experiments fail to evaluate all single-component baselines (e.g., evaluating context-aware decoding 'C' in isolation or dual mapping 'B' in isolation), making it difficult to rigorously determine the independent utility of each module.

Presentation and writing flaws: The manuscript contains multiple conspicuous grammatical and spelling errors in prominent locations, including the title ('FULLY INTEGRATION' instead of 'FULL INTEGRATION'), abstract ('a fully vision-language alignment'), benchmark tables ('Cambrain 8B' in Table 1), section headers ('SynthSpaital' in Table 16), and prompts ('shuold' in Table 28).
